cards.titel: Nerve action potential (NAP) recording across a lesion in continuity
cards.notiz: Greenberg Table 30.8, p. 535. ≥ 60% of nerve injuries are in continuity. A NAP distal to the lesion (any amplitude) means regeneration → neurolysis only; no NAP → resect and graft.

cards.text: The **24-month rule**: after about {{c1::24 months}} of denervation most muscles cannot regain useful function even if reinnervated, because of {{c2::motor end-plate degeneration and fibrosis}}. Exceptions: {{c3::facial muscles and large bulky muscles (biceps, brachialis, gastrocnemius)}}. The farther the injury from the target muscle, the {{c4::earlier}} repair should be considered.

cards.rueckseite:
Paroxysmal stabbing pain in the distribution of the **greater (or lesser) occipital nerve** (C2), from the suboccipital region over the vertex, ± tenderness and **Tinel sign** over the nerve.
**Causes:** entrapment in the trapezius/semispinalis, trauma, C1–2 arthrosis, Chiari, tumors; differential: C2 radiculopathy, migraine, cervicogenic headache.
**Diagnosis:** relief with **local anesthetic block**.
**Treatment:** blocks/steroid, neuropathic drugs; refractory: occipital nerve decompression, neurectomy, C2 ganglionectomy, occipital nerve stimulation.

Branch of the **posterior cord** (C5–C6) through the **quadrilateral space**.
**Causes:** anterior **shoulder dislocation**, proximal humerus fracture, quadrilateral space syndrome (fibrous bands, throwing athletes), crutches.
**Signs:** weak **deltoid** (abduction 30–90°) and teres minor (external rotation), numbness over the lateral shoulder ("regimental badge" area).

**Femoral (L2–L4):** weak knee extension (and hip flexion if above the inguinal ligament), **lost knee jerk**, numbness of the anterior thigh/medial leg (saphenous). Causes: **retroperitoneal (iliopsoas) hematoma** on anticoagulation, lithotomy positioning, hip surgery, pelvic retractors, **diabetic amyotrophy**.
**Obturator (L2–L4):** weak **adduction**, medial thigh numbness; causes: pelvic fracture, obturator hernia, pelvic surgery, labor.
L4 radiculopathy instead also weakens tibialis anterior.

Acute **severe shoulder/arm pain** for days, followed as the pain subsides by **patchy weakness** and atrophy (often serratus anterior → winged scapula, deltoid, spinati, AIN), sensory loss usually minor.
Triggers: infection, vaccination, surgery, pregnancy; hereditary form (SEPT9).
MRI of the spine is normal (key differential: cervical radiculopathy). EMG after 3–4 weeks shows patchy denervation.
Treatment: analgesia, steroids early, physical therapy; recovery over months to 2–3 years in most.

Pain then weakness in several root/nerve territories of the leg, not explained by one root.
**Causes:** **diabetic amyotrophy** (diabetic lumbosacral radiculoplexus neuropathy: older type 2 diabetics, weight loss, asymmetric proximal thigh pain and weakness), **retroperitoneal hematoma** (anticoagulation), tumor infiltration (colorectal, cervical, prostate, lymphoma), radiation plexopathy, pregnancy/delivery, aortic surgery.
Work-up: EMG (paraspinals spared in plexopathy), MRI of the plexus, CT for hematoma.

zeilen: Distal weakness, reduced sensation, hyporeflexia; failure to wean
Proximal and distal weakness, sensation normal
Low CMAP, **normal SNAP**; muscle not excitable by direct stimulation
cards.notiz: Greenberg p. 569 (and p. 193). Both delay ventilator weaning; recovery over weeks to months.

cards.rueckseite:
≈ 1/3 of anesthesia malpractice claims; most often **ulnar nerve** and **brachial plexus**.
**Ulnar:** men, obesity, prolonged postop bed rest; often symptoms appear > 48 h after surgery and many have contralateral subclinical neuropathy (not just positioning).
**Brachial plexus:** arm abducted > 90°, sternotomy, head turned away.
**Others:** peroneal (lateral positioning, stirrups), lateral femoral cutaneous (prone, iliac pads), sciatic (lithotomy), facial/supraorbital (pins, masks), **ION/POVL** (blindness after prone spine surgery).
Prevent with padding, neutral positions, abduction < 90°.

zeilen: **Cervicomedullary junction** (Chiari I, basilar impression, foramen magnum tumor, syrinx); also drugs (phenytoin, carbamazepine, lithium), Wernicke, Mg deficiency
Diencephalon / parasellar mass, chiasm (with bitemporal hemianopia)
Large CPA tumor: coarse gaze-evoked toward the lesion, fine vestibular away from it

cards.rueckseite:
Disc swelling from **raised ICP** (bilateral by definition); vision is preserved early (enlarged blind spot), unlike optic neuritis.
**Funduscopy:** loss of **spontaneous venous pulsations** (absent in 10–20% of normals, so their presence argues against raised ICP), blurred margins, hyperemia, obscured vessels at the disc margin, peripapillary hemorrhages, cotton wool spots, later atrophy (pale disc).
It takes **hours to days** to develop (24–48 h); can persist for weeks after ICP normalizes.
**Imaging:** flattening of the posterior globe, distended optic nerve sheath, empty sella, tortuous nerve.
**Pseudopapilledema:** drusen, hyperopia, tilted discs.

Pupillomotor fibers lie **superficially (dorsomedially)** with their own blood supply.
- **Compressive** (PComm/ICA aneurysm, uncal herniation): **pupil involved early**; painful → urgent CTA
- **Ischemic/diabetic** (vasa nervorum, core of the nerve): **pupil spared** in ≈ 80%, pain common, recovers in 2–3 months
- Rule: complete motor palsy with a normal pupil is rarely an aneurysm; a partial palsy with a spared pupil still needs imaging
- **Aberrant regeneration** (lid elevation on adduction/depression) implies compression (aneurysm, tumor), not ischemia

cards.vorderseite: Trochlear and abducens palsy: causes and tests
cards.rueckseite:
**IV:** vertical diplopia worse looking down and in (stairs, reading); head tilt **away** from the lesion; **Parks–Bielschowsky three-step test**. Most common cause: **head trauma** (often bilateral), then congenital (decompensated), microvascular.
**VI:** horizontal diplopia worse at distance and toward the lesion. Causes: raised ICP (false localizing), low ICP (after LP), microvascular, clivus tumors (chordoma), Gradenigo, cavernous sinus lesions, Wernicke; in children postviral.

**Tolosa–Hunt:** nonspecific (granulomatous) inflammation of the **superior orbital fissure/cavernous sinus** → painful ophthalmoplegia (any of III, IV, VI, V1), **pupil usually spared**, days to weeks, recurs, no systemic involvement; **dramatic response to steroids** (prednisone 60–80 mg) within ≈ 1 day. A diagnosis of exclusion (MRI, rule out tumor, aneurysm, lymphoma, fungal infection).
**Raeder paratrigeminal neuralgia:** **partial Horner** (no anhidrosis) + ipsilateral **V1 pain**; lesion in the middle fossa next to the trigeminal nerve (rarely ICA aneurysm/dissection).
Other differentials: carotid-cavernous fistula, cavernous sinus thrombosis, diabetic III, orbital pseudotumor.

**Endolymphatic hydrops.**
**Clinic:** episodic **vertigo** (20 min to hours), **fluctuating low-frequency sensorineural hearing loss**, **tinnitus**, **aural fullness**; progressive hearing loss over years, bilateral in up to 30–50%.
**Treatment:** low-salt diet, diuretics, betahistine; intratympanic steroids or **gentamicin** (chemical labyrinthectomy); surgery: endolymphatic sac decompression, **vestibular neurectomy** (preserves hearing) or labyrinthectomy (if no useful hearing).

zeilen: Mild dysfunction: slight weakness on close inspection, complete eye closure with minimal effort
Moderate: obvious but not disfiguring asymmetry, synkinesis; **complete eye closure with effort**, forehead movement present
Moderately severe: disfiguring asymmetry, **incomplete eye closure**, no forehead movement
cards.notiz: Greenberg Table 45.3 (p. 607). Used to report outcome after vestibular schwannoma surgery; I–II is considered good.

cards.rueckseite:
Idiopathic peripheral facial palsy (likely **HSV** reactivation); 50–80% of peripheral facial palsies, a **diagnosis of exclusion** (no other cranial nerve, systemic or tumor signs).
Prodrome; complete at onset in 50%, otherwise maximal within 1 week; retroauricular pain (60%), dysgeusia, hyperacusis.
**Treatment:** **prednisone** within 72 h (± valacyclovir), **eye protection**.
**Prognosis:** most recover; worse with complete palsy, age, no recovery by 3 weeks. **Progression after 3 weeks or no recovery by 4–6 months → MRI** (rule out tumor, e.g., facial schwannoma, parotid malignancy).
Ramsay Hunt (zoster oticus): vesicles in the ear canal, worse prognosis; Lyme: often bilateral.

zeilen: BC > AC on the affected side (negative)
cards.notiz: Greenberg p. 611. Unilateral sensorineural loss or asymmetric hearing needs MRI to rule out vestibular schwannoma.
